text: Attackers can bypass application logic on dual-use endpoints by omitting mandatory parameters. When multiple operations are handled by a single controller or script, parameter presence acts as an implicit router. Deleting a parameter name or its value can force the backend into unhandled fallback routines, alternative code branches, or privilege escalation paths.

metadata.title: Parameter Omission and Dual-Use Endpoint Exploitation
metadata.technique: Systematic parameter removal across GET, POST, and Cookie headers
execution_steps: Intercept request using an HTTP proxy
Remove one parameter at a time (both key and value)
Submit and inspect response diffs for fallback routing
Trace multi-stage workflows to identify state desynchronization

text: Forced browsing and step skipping in multi-stage workflows allow attackers to reach terminal states without satisfying intermediate requirements. For instance, in two-factor authentication (Login -> 2FA Prompt -> Account Dashboard), directly invoking the post-2FA endpoint via forced browsing circumvents token submission when the server relies on client navigation order instead of server-side state enforcement.

metadata.title: State Sequence Violation and Workflow Step-Skipping
metadata.flawed_assumption: Users will sequentially advance through pages in the order dictated by the client interface.
associated_labs: Authentication bypass via flawed state machine (Practitioner)

text: In e-commerce workflows, state desynchronization occurs when cart adjustment calculations do not recalculate discounts after cart modification. An attacker adds items to exceed a discount threshold (e.g., $1000 for 10% off), applies the coupon, and subsequently removes the items; if the server fails to verify preconditions upon checkout, the discount persists on the smaller total.

metadata.title: State Desynchronization in Post-Condition Order Discounts

rule_constraints.invariant: cart.subtotal >= 1000 must hold at checkout execution

metadata.vulnerability_mechanism: Missing re-validation of pricing invariants when cart mutation occurs in intermediate state.

text: In a purchasing workflow, the client browser transmits the item unit price directly within the POST request payload when adding items to the cart. Because the server fails to validate the price against a database source of truth, an attacker intercepting the request can manipulate the price parameter to an arbitrary low value (e.g., less than available store credit), enabling checkout completion without adequate funds.

metadata.title: Arbitrary Price Tampering via Client-Supplied Parameter
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security
attack_steps: Authenticate with standard credentials.
Attempt order to determine insufficient credit ceiling.
Intercept 'POST /cart' request containing client-specified 'price' parameter.
Tamper 'price' value to an arbitrary lower integer within balance limit.
Submit order via checkout endpoint to complete purchase.

text: Pattern: Transaction Total Manipulation via Negative Item Quantities. In an e-commerce purchasing workflow, an add-to-cart or cart-update endpoint accepts user-controlled item quantities without validating that the integer is strictly positive. When a negative quantity is supplied, the application performs signed arithmetic on both the line item and total order calculations (item_total = price * quantity). An attacker can add an expensive target item to the cart, then add a calculated negative quantity of another product to reduce the overall order subtotal to an arbitrary low or negative value, bypassing store credit or balance limits during checkout. Example Trace: Intercept POST /cart, submit 'productId=2' with 'quantity=-10' alongside the target high-value product, reducing the cart subtotal below available store credit, and execute checkout.

metadata.title: Cart Subtotal Reduction via Negative Quantity Injection
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-1284: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input
attack_steps: Authenticate with standard buyer credentials.
Add expensive target item (e.g., leather jacket) to cart.
Intercept cart addition request for a secondary item.
Inject a negative integer value into the quantity parameter.
Verify that the subtotal is reduced by (unit_price * |negative_quantity|).
Balance the equation so 0 < total_price <= user_credit.
Complete checkout.

text: Pattern: Inconsistent Security Controls via Post-Registration Identity Mutation. The application restricts privileged functionality (e.g., administrative panels) based on user email domain matching. While initial account registration enforces domain restrictions or requires domain verification (e.g., email confirmation links), secondary account management workflows (such as updating profile email) lack the same domain validation or re-verification controls. An attacker registers with an arbitrary permitted domain, updates their email address to a privileged domain (e.g., @company.com) via user settings, and bypasses administrative access barriers.

metadata.title: Privilege Escalation via Inconsistent Email Domain Verification
attack_steps: Enumerate restricted/admin interfaces to identify access requirements or privileged domains from error messages.
Register a standard account using a legitimate/controllable domain and complete email activation.
Authenticate and navigate to secondary profile update functionality.
Update account email address directly to the privileged target domain (e.g., victim-corp.com) without undergoing re-verification.
Access restricted administrative endpoints with elevated privileges.
Execute administrative actions (e.g., user deletion).

concrete_example.mutation_action: Update email to @dontwannacry.com via account settings

text: Pattern: Coupon Replay via State History Naivety (Alternating Code Application). In checkout workflows, an application enforces single-use constraints on promotional discount coupons by only comparing incoming coupon submissions against the most recently applied coupon code (last_applied_coupon != current_coupon) rather than maintaining an aggregated set or transaction-level redemption ledger. An attacker alternates submissions between two or more valid coupon codes (e.g., CODE_A -> CODE_B -> CODE_A -> CODE_B), repeatedly resetting the immediate state check and compounding discounts until the order total is reduced to an arbitrary low value or zero.

metadata.title: Compounded Discount Abuse via Alternating Coupon Application
attack_steps: Acquire multiple distinct promotional discount codes.
Add target items to cart.
Submit first coupon code (e.g., POST /cart/coupon with NEWCUST5).
Attempt duplicate submission of same code to confirm immediate rejection.
Submit alternate coupon code (e.g., SIGNUP30).
Alternately resubmit both codes in sequence (A -> B -> A -> B) to continuously depress order total below available credit.
Complete checkout order.

text: Pattern: Financial Total Manipulation via 32-Bit Signed Integer Overflow. An application enforces superficial limits on input quantity parameters (e.g., maximum 2-digit integer per request), but fails to enforce upper bounds or overflow protections on the cumulative cart balance stored in primitive integer types (such as a 32-bit signed int, INT_MAX = 2,147,483,647 cents). An attacker repeatedly dispatches item addition requests (e.g., quantity=99) using automated request flooding. Once cumulative total exceeds INT_MAX, the variable wraps around to the negative boundary (INT_MIN = -2,147,483,648). The attacker precisely calculates payload iterations and auxiliary item offsets to settle the wrapped subtotal into a valid positive range below available store credit, completing checkout below true cost.

metadata.title: Integer Overflow in Financial Aggregation Logic
attack_steps: Identify per-request quantity input validation ceiling (e.g., 2-digit ceiling).
Observe total financial value representation (e.g., stored internally in cents).
Utilize automated request generation (e.g., Burp Intruder Null Payloads) with serial concurrency (pool=1) to increment line items toward 32-bit signed limit (2,147,483,647).
Verify integer wraparound occurs when total flips to negative boundary (-2,147,483,648).
Calculate required payload count to settle wrapped negative balance near zero.
Inject auxiliary item quantities to offset negative balance into the target payable window ($0 < total <= balance).
Submit order checkout to acquire target products.

text: Pattern: Privilege Escalation via String Truncation Discrepancy (Database Storage vs Validation Layer). An application uses the recipient email address for two distinct operations: sending out-of-band account activation tokens via SMTP, and evaluating user domain authorization in the administrative access controller. The validation and mail-routing layers support long email strings without length enforcement, while the database storage layer silently truncates strings exceeding a fixed column capacity (e.g., VARCHAR(255)). An attacker constructs a crafted email address where the subdomain segment matches the privileged corporate domain (e.g., prefix@target-corp.com.attacker-domain.tld) padded precisely so the 255th character aligns with the end of the corporate domain. The email server routes the activation token to the attacker's full domain, while database persistence clips the attacker's trailing domain, converting the stored identity into a verified corporate user with administrative access.

metadata.title: Privilege Escalation via Email Truncation and Domain Boundary Clipping
metadata.state_transition: UNREGISTERED -> REGISTRATION_SUBMITTED (Long String) -> TOKEN_DELIVERED (Full Domain) -> ACCOUNT_PERSISTED (Truncated Domain) -> ADMIN_ACCESS_GRANTED
attack_steps: Probe registration with an oversized email address (>200 chars) to observe storage behavior on profile reflection.
Identify storage boundary truncation (e.g., string sliced at exactly 255 characters).
Calculate padding length: prefix_len + len('@privileged-domain.com') == truncation_limit (255).
Construct payload: [padding]@[privileged-domain.com].[attacker-controlled-domain].
Submit registration; activation email routes to attacker control via full DNS hierarchy.
Complete verification via confirmation link.
Authenticate to verify stored email clipped to target domain (@privileged-domain.com).
Access administrative panel and invoke privileged actions.

text: Pattern: Privilege Escalation via Parameter Omission on Dual-Use Endpoints. A single backend controller handles password modification for both self-service user updates and administrative overrides. The application relies on the presence of the 'current-password' parameter to infer whether the caller is a standard user (requiring existing credential validation) or an administrator (bypassing verification). Additionally, the target user identity is derived from a client-controllable 'username' parameter rather than strictly binding to the authenticated session context. An attacker removes the 'current-password' parameter entirely and overrides the 'username' parameter with a privileged account (e.g., 'administrator'), causing the backend to execute the administrative override branch and overwrite the target account's password without prior authentication.

metadata.title: Arbitrary Password Reset via Dual-Use Endpoint Parameter Omission
metadata.state_transition: AUTHENTICATED_LOW_PRIV -> DISPATCH_DUAL_USE_ACTION (Omitted Verification Param + Mutated Target Identity) -> TARGET_ACCOUNT_COMPROMISED -> PRIVILEGED_SESSION_ACQUIRED
attack_steps: Authenticate with low-privilege credentials and perform a baseline password change.
Inspect the HTTP request (e.g., POST /my-account/change-password).
Observe dual-use parameters: 'username', 'current-password', and 'new-password-1'.
Omit the 'current-password' parameter entirely to test for execution branch switching.
Verify that password change succeeds without current credential validation.
Inject a target high-privilege account identifier into 'username' (e.g., username=administrator).
Submit the request and authenticate as the targeted user using the newly established password.

text: Pattern: Forced Browsing and Workflow Step-Skipping in Purchasing Checkout. The purchasing state machine improperly assumes that navigating to the terminal confirmation endpoint can only occur after successful payment settlement. The server-side fulfillment handler evaluates the GET /cart/order-confirmation?order-confirmation=true request as an authoritative completion trigger rather than verifying that the active session's cart successfully completed the transactional payment stage (e.g., POST /cart/checkout). An attacker populates the cart with high-value items and directly replays the order-confirmation request, completing order fulfillment without initiating the payment or deduction routine.

metadata.title: Purchasing Workflow Step-Skipping via Direct Confirmation Invocations
attack_steps: Complete a baseline purchase of an affordable item to map normal workflow progression.
Inspect proxy history and record terminal confirmation request (e.g., GET /cart/order-confirmation?order-confirmation=true).
Add targeted high-value item to the cart.
Bypass intermediate payment submission endpoints entirely using forced browsing to directly issue the recorded confirmation request.
Verify that the order moves to confirmed state without financial balance deduction.

text: Pattern: Authentication Bypass via Partial Workflow Abort / State Machine Dropping. An application implements a multi-step authentication flow: credential verification followed by intermediate role assignment (POST /login -> GET /role-selector -> POST /role-selector -> Home). The backend initializes the session state with an implicit or unconstrained privileged role (e.g., admin) immediately upon credential verification, assuming the subsequent role-selector step will safely downgrade or explicitly set the user's intended role. By intercepting and dropping the intermediate transition request (GET /role-selector) and navigating directly to the application core, the attacker halts workflow progression before the unprivileged role assignment takes place, retaining the default elevated state.

metadata.title: Authentication Bypass and Privilege Default via Dropped State Transition
metadata.state_transition: UNAUTHENTICATED -> CREDENTIALS_VALIDATED (Default State: Admin) -> [GET /role-selector DROPPED] -> ROLE_INITIALIZATION_ABORTED -> PRIVILEGED_DASHBOARD_ACCESSED
attack_steps: Authenticate with baseline unprivileged credentials (wiener:peter) and map multi-step login sequence.
Identify role-selection intermediate state (/role-selector) preceding landing dashboard.
Identify restricted administration paths (e.g., /admin) via content discovery.
Re-authenticate while intercepting traffic in an HTTP proxy.
Forward initial credential submission (POST /login).
Intercept and drop the follow-up intermediate request (GET /role-selector).
Directly browse to the target root / home page using the active session.
Verify session inherits default unconstrained administrative role and execute admin actions.

text: Pattern: Infinite Currency Arbitrage via Reusable Discount on Cash-Equivalent Instruments. An application permits generic promotional discount codes (e.g., 30% off) to apply to cash-equivalent instruments such as gift cards or store vouchers. When a user purchases a gift card of face value $V at discounted cost $C (where C < V) using store credit and subsequently redeems the newly issued voucher into the same store credit balance, the net account balance increases by (V - C) per cycle. By chaining this loop within an automated macro or concurrency runner (Cart Addition -> Apply Discount -> Checkout -> Extract Issued Voucher -> Redeem Voucher), an attacker generates unbounded store credit without introducing external capital.

metadata.title: Infinite Store Credit Generation via Discounted Gift Card Arbitrage
metadata.state_transition: INITIAL_BALANCE -> GIFT_CARD_PURCHASE_DISCOUNTED -> ORDER_FULFILLED -> VOUCHER_REDEEMED -> INFLATED_BALANCE -> LOOP_REPEAT
attack_steps: Acquire reusable or self-service promotional coupon (e.g., SIGNUP30 granting 30% discount).
Add cash-equivalent item (e.g., $10 gift card) to shopping cart.
Apply discount coupon to reduce checkout total below card face value ($7 instead of $10).
Complete purchase using current store credit.
Extract issued gift card code from fulfillment response (GET /cart/order-confirmation).
Submit redemption request (POST /gift-card) to credit full face value ($10) back to account balance.
Automate the multi-step cycle via macro/script to compound store credit iteratively until targeted financial ceiling is met.

text: Pattern: Authentication Bypass via Dual Encryption/Decryption Oracle and Ciphertext Manipulation. An application reuses identical cryptographic keys, algorithms, and block-cipher modes across distinct functional domains (e.g., transient UI notifications and persistent authentication session cookies). When an unhandled error path reflects decrypted user input (decryption oracle via notification cookie) and a validation failure path returns encrypted user input in a cookie (encryption oracle via email error handler), an attacker decrypts their legitimate session token to identify its structural schema (e.g., username:timestamp). The attacker then encrypts an arbitrary target payload (administrator:timestamp). Because the application prefixes error inputs with static text ('Invalid email address: '), the attacker pads the payload so the prefix and padding align to cipher block boundaries (e.g., 16-byte blocks in CBC/ECB mode). Slicing off the initial 32 bytes of ciphertext eliminates the prefix without invalidating the trailing target ciphertext block, forging a valid persistent administrator session token.

metadata.title: Authentication Cookie Forgery via Symmetric Encryption Oracle and Block Truncation
metadata.state_transition: AUTHENTICATED_LOW_PRIV -> ORACLE_KEY_REUSE_DISCOVERED -> CIPHERTEXT_DECRYPTED (Schema Extracted) -> PADDED_TARGET_ENCRYPTED -> CIPHER_BLOCK_SLICED -> ADMIN_SESSION_FORGED -> ADMIN_ACCESS_GRANTED
attack_steps: Log in with persistent session enabled ('Stay logged in') and capture the encrypted 'stay-logged-in' cookie.
Submit invalid input into a secondary endpoint (e.g., invalid email in comment form) to trigger error tracking via encrypted 'notification' cookie.
Observe that retrieving the target post decrypts the 'notification' cookie and reflects the plaintext string, establishing a decryption oracle.
Feed 'stay-logged-in' ciphertext into the 'notification' parameter to decrypt the token and discover its format: username:timestamp.
Note that the encryption oracle prepends a 23-byte static prefix ('Invalid email address: ').
Calculate block alignment padding: 23 bytes prefix + 9 padding bytes = 32 bytes (exact multiple of 16-byte block cipher).
Submit padded payload (xxxxxxxxxadministrator:timestamp) to the encryption oracle (email parameter) and capture the resulting ciphertext.
Decode Base64 ciphertext, remove the first 32 bytes (2 cipher blocks), re-encode to Base64, and verify via decryption oracle that only 'administrator:timestamp' remains.
Replace 'stay-logged-in' cookie with the forged ciphertext to authenticate as administrator and access privileged endpoints.

text: Pattern: Access Control and Domain Validation Bypass via Email Encoded-Word (RFC 2047) Parser Discrepancy. An application restricts user registration and administrative privileges to an authoritative internal domain (e.g., ginandjuice.shop) by inspecting the trailing domain substring of incoming email addresses. The front-end validation layer detects common MIME Encoded-Word formats (e.g., =?iso-8859-1?q?...?= and =?utf-8?q?...?=) but fails to blacklist or normalize legacy encodings such as UTF-7 (RFC 1642 / RFC 2152, =?utf-7?q?...?=). An attacker crafts an email payload embedding their actual external address and delimiter characters inside an unhandled UTF-7 encoded-word block while affixing the required corporate domain as an external suffix: =?utf-7?q?attacker&AEA-[EXPLOIT_HOST]&ACA-?=@target-corp.com. The registration validation check interprets the trailing unencoded @target-corp.com as compliant, whereas the underlying downstream mail-transfer agent (MTA) or SMTP client decodes the embedded UTF-7 delimiter (&AEA- -> @, &ACA- -> space) and routes the out-of-band activation token to the attacker-controlled server. Upon link verification, the backend derives privileged access based on the verified corporate domain identity.

metadata.title: Registration Domain Bypass via RFC 2047 UTF-7 MIME Encoding Discrepancy
metadata.state_transition: UNAUTHENTICATED -> ENCODED_REGISTRATION_SUBMITTED (UTF-7 Encoded Delimiters) -> DOMAIN_CHECK_PASSED -> OUT_OF_BAND_TOKEN_ROUTED_ATTACKER -> ACCOUNT_ACTIVATED -> ADMIN_ACCESS_GRANTED
attack_steps: Submit baseline registration using an unauthorized external domain to identify target domain constraints from the failure response.
Test encoded-word MIME encapsulation using standard charsets (=?iso-8859-1?=, =?utf-8?=) to detect security filter signatures.
Identify filter discrepancy by injecting legacy charsets (e.g., =?utf-7?=) that evade the pattern-matching filter without triggering rejection.
Encode the attacker's delivery domain and separator characters into UTF-7 representation (&AEA- for '@', &ACA- for space).
Append the mandatory corporate domain as the outer unencoded suffix: =?utf-7?q?attacker&AEA-[EXPLOIT_HOST]&ACA-?=@target-domain.com.
Submit registration; confirm that out-of-band activation email arrives at the attacker's mail server via decoded MTA routing.
Activate the account using the confirmation link and log in to inherit privileged administrative rights.

text: Overview of Email Atom Splitting and Parser Discrepancies: Email parsing standards (RFC 2822 / RFC 5322) incorporate complex behaviors including quoted local-parts, comments, escape sequences, and multi-layer MIME encodings (e.g., encoded-words, Punycode, UUCP, and source routes). Because web applications farm out email validation and parsing to diverse libraries without knowing how downstream mail transfer agents (MTAs) interpret the input, discrepancies arise. Attackers exploit these gaps to route emails to unexpected destinations, bypass domain-based access controls on platforms like GitHub, Zendesk, and GitLab, or trigger code execution vulnerabilities such as style tag injection and CSS exfiltration leading to RCE in Joomla (CVE-2024-21725).

metadata.title: Splitting the Email Atom: Exploiting Parsers to Bypass Access Controls
metadata.impact: Access Control Bypass, Cloudflare Zero Trust IdP Impersonation, and Remote Code Execution via CSS Exfiltration.

text: Pattern: Email Domain Confusion via Archaic Protocol Invocations. Email routing parsers and mailers (such as Sendmail and Postfix) inherit support for legacy protocols predating modern internet standards, including UUCP (Unix To Unix Copy, using exclamation mark separators) and source-chaining percent hacks/source routes. By injecting escape characters, double quotes, and archaic separators (e.g., ! or %), an attacker creates confusion between the validation layer and the underlying mail transfer agent. This causes the application validation layer to treat the address as belonging to an allowed domain while the mailer routes the message or out-of-band verification token to an attacker-controlled external mail server.

metadata.title: Email Domain Confusion via UUCP and Source Routes

text: Pattern: Email Splitting via MIME Encoded-Word (RFC 2047). Applications relying on libraries like Ruby's 'Mail' gem parse and decode RFC 2047 encoded-word sequences (=?charset?encoding?encoded-text?=) within email addresses. Attackers encode characters such as raw at-symbols (=40), command termination characters (=3e for greater-than), and null bytes (=00) to terminate SMTP commands prematurely or inject secondary mailbox destinations. This passes front-end domain regex validation while splitting the recipient specification during MTA transmission, allowing attackers to forge verified domain ownership on platforms like GitHub, Zendesk, and GitLab.

metadata.title: Email Splitting via MIME Encoded-Word Discrepancies

text: Pattern: Remote Code Execution via Punycode Malformation and CSS Exfiltration (CVE-2024-21725). Defective PHP IDN libraries mishandle malformed Punycode sequences containing non-standard digit combinations (e.g., xn--0049, xn--42), decoding them into unintended characters like opening angle brackets and style tags. When output in vulnerable applications like Joomla, this injects an unclosed HTML style tag into user list pages. An attacker registers two accounts: the first injects the malicious Punycode domain opening a style tag, and the second injects CSS import statements using curly braces to neutralize subsequent HTML. Combined with a custom CSS exfiltration tool, this steals super administrator CSRF tokens, enabling automated modification of backend templates to achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE).

metadata.title: RCE via Punycode Malformation, Style Injection, and CSS Exfiltration in Joomla
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
attack_steps: Identify IDN library decoding flaw in PHP application
Register account 1 with malformed Punycode generating unclosed HTML style tags
Register account 2 containing CSS import rules and curly braces to neutralize trailing HTML
Harvest administrator CSRF token via blind CSS exfiltration stylesheet
Forge administrative request to edit backend PHP template and achieve RCE

text: Pattern: Common Business Logic Abuse Cases across State Machines. 1) State-Desynchronized Parameter Manipulation: An attacker moves through checkout to a review/summary state, resets or injects lower financial parameters, and completes purchase without backend price re-verification. 2) Resource Locking Arbitrage: An attacker initiates transactions to lock out or exhaust inventory/resources, starving competing users or driving price deflation. 3) Transaction Rollback Asymmetry: An attacker executes a state transition that awards credits, loyalty points, or secondary benefits, and subsequently cancels or rolls back the parent transaction while the secondary benefit persists due to lack of cross-state transactional atomicity.

metadata.title: Representative Business Logic Abuse and Misuse Patterns
prerequisites: Client control over transaction state sequence
Non-atomic handling of state rollback operations

text: Pattern: Exploitation of Business Logic Data Handoffs and Validation Gaps. 1) Multi-Tier Routing Manipulation: In split-fulfillment workflows (e.g., in-stock warehouse fulfillment vs. dropship partner fulfillment), an attacker mutates internal routing parameters to redirect an in-stock order to a partner fulfillment queue, or directly invokes partner fulfillment APIs without payment confirmation. 2) State Latency and Batch Replay Race Conditions: In systems relying on asynchronous or nightly balance synchronization (e.g., credit card ledger caching), an attacker executes rapid concurrent transactions across geographically distributed endpoints, exceeding credit or debit ceilings before batch balance reconciliation occurs. 3) Distributed Denial of Dollar (DDo$): Attackers exploit asymmetric fee schedules by sending high-frequency micro-transactions (e.g., 1 SEK donations), exhausting free transaction quotas and forcing target accounts to incur per-transaction surcharges that exceed the transferred value.

metadata.title: Multi-Tier Data Injection, Batch Latency, and Economic DDo$ Abuse
prerequisites: Fixed transaction surcharge threshold without floor bounds

text: Pattern: Direct Parameter Manipulation and Debug Feature Activation via Request Forgery. 1) Single-Use Discount Flag Reset: An e-commerce system utilizes an in-flight parameter (e.g., is_discount_applied=0) to evaluate eligibility. An attacker intercepts the submission and forces the flag to remain 0 across successive requests, compounding single-use discounts. 2) Gamification and Reward Multiplier Bypassing: An attacker exposes hidden development fields (e.g., level_skip=true, god_mode=1) to advance application state and accumulate premium assets or tokens without completing prerequisite tasks. 3) Information Leakage via Telemetry Flags: Injecting latent debug parameters (e.g., debug=true, show_coords=1) reveals sensitive backend state or competitor positions.

metadata.title: State Flag Overriding and Hidden Parameter Manipulation
attack_steps: Observe baseline requests across transactions via intercepting proxy.
Identify hidden input fields, boolean state flags, or predictable numeric parameters.
Tamper state flags to false or unconsumed values to replay single-use business operations.
Inject speculative parameters (e.g., debug=1, test=true, admin=true) to evaluate backend branch execution.
Verify whether privileges or financial balances update without valid operational checks.

text: Pattern: Parameter Injection into Restricted or Non-Editable Fields. 1) Privileged Field Injection: An administrative password change interface conditionally suppresses target username inputs on unprivileged views. An unprivileged user proxies the submission, appends 'username=target_user' and 'new_password=val', tricking backend logic into executing a privileged identity update. 2) Relational Selector IDOR / Scoping Tampering: A project management portal limits user visibility via a populated HTML dropdown. An attacker intercepts the request, replaces the authorized project ID with an arbitrary foreign project ID, and bypasses scoping checks due to missing relational authorization. 3) Semantic Relational Corruption: In multi-attribute profile systems (e.g., citizen records), an attacker submits conflicting relation pairs (e.g., marital_status='single' while supplying spouse_name='John Doe') to corrupt referential data integrity in persistent storage. 4) Audit Log Tampering: Attackers access or mutate backend log stores to destroy forensic integrity or inject misleading trace records.

metadata.title: UI-Restricted Field Injection and Referential Integrity Corruption
attack_steps: Map application UI elements to discover hidden, disabled, or conditionally rendered form parameters.
Inspect baseline HTTP request payloads using an intercepting proxy to identify differences between client DOM constraints and backend parameter handlers.
Inject parameters that are non-editable or hidden in the current user's session context.
Substitute relational foreign identifiers (e.g., project_id, organization_id) to verify if cross-tenant scoping is enforced server-side.
Submit mutually contradictory relational data attributes to evaluate backend referential validation.

text: Pattern: Exploitation of Process Timing and State Window Latency. 1) Authentication Timing Side-Channel: An attacker measures round-trip response latencies on login endpoints; operations executing password hash algorithms only for existing users exhibit statistically significant higher latency, enabling username enumeration. 2) Resource Locking and Inventory Starvation: In seat allocation or ticketing platforms, initiating checkout reserves seats without settlement. Stalling the transaction without timeouts locks out legitimate buyers. 3) Market Price Arbitrage via Stalled Checkout: In commodity or asset trading workflows where spot prices fluctuate, an attacker acquires a favorable quote at $T_0$, stalls the transaction, monitors market movements, and completes settlement at $T_1$ only if the market price has risen, locking in an outdated discount.

metadata.title: Timing Side-Channels, Inventory Starvation, and Stalled Arbitrage
attack_steps: Map endpoints with execution paths dependent on external variables or internal verification tiers.
Analyze response time distributions using statistical timing probes to identify user or state enumeration.
Initiate resource reservation requests and pause interaction to identify maximum hold timeout boundaries.
Capture time-sensitive price quotes and defer final order submission across market fluctuation intervals to test quote validity enforcement.

text: Pattern: Function Limit Bypass and Quota Exhaustion via Navigation Replay. In an e-commerce checkout workflow, users are granted a single-use discount applied once per order. An attacker navigates forward to cart review, then navigates backward or replays the discount application endpoint repeatedly using an intercepting proxy. If the backend fails to bind the applied discount to an immutable transaction state or update the coupon status to 'REDEEMED' at the database tier, the attacker compounds multiple discounts or stacks the same discount multiple times onto a single order total.

metadata.title: Promotional Discount Stacking via Function Limit Bypass
attack_steps: Identify operations tied to consumption quotas (e.g., promotional codes, document downloads, reward redemptions).
Execute initial invocation to consume the allowable limit.
Replay the request directly via an intercepting proxy without completing subsequent lifecycle transitions.
Test multi-stage navigation loops (back-and-forth traversal, cart emptying and reloading) to observe if limits reset.
Verify whether cumulative benefits exceed established business policy allowances.

text: Pattern: Workflow Subversion and Rollback Asymmetry. 1) Premature Loyalty/Credit Accrual with Transaction Rollback: In a purchasing flow, initiating an order triggers an immediate increment of reward points or store credits. The attacker aborts or cancels the transaction before final payment tender, or mutates the basket to zero; the parent transaction terminates, but the auxiliary loyalty credits persist because the rollback operation is decoupled. 2) Content Policy Evasion via Secondary Edit: A content submission engine validates incoming text against a denylist (e.g., profanity or restricted keywords) on POST /create, but the corresponding PUT/PATCH /edit endpoint fails to re-execute content filters. An attacker posts benign content to establish the entry, then updates the post with restricted text to bypass publishing policies.

metadata.title: Reward Point Arbitrage and Post-Validation Policy Evasion
attack_steps: Map target workflow to identify intermediate steps that trigger side-effects (e.g., awarding points, allocating temporary quotas).
Advance the state to trigger the award.
Prematurely abort, cancel, or reduce final tender amount before settlement.
Verify if auxiliary assets remain credited in the user profile.
Test secondary lifecycle routes (e.g., edit, draft update) with restricted payloads to verify if initial creation filters are skipped.

text: Pattern: Progressive Anomaly Injection to Evaluate Application Self-Defense. An attacker executes a series of low-frequency, structurally anomalous, or unauthorized interactions across an authenticated session: 1) Probing restricted resource IDs outside the user's role (forced browsing / IDOR). 2) Injecting syntax delimiters into numeric fields (e.g., tick marks). 3) Mutating HTTP request methods (GET to POST). 4) Injecting duplicate or extra parameters. 5) Dispatching rapid, out-of-order workflow calls or high-frequency functional submissions (e.g., voucher codes, failed payments). If the application fails to alter its defensive posture (e.g., imposing progressive delays, stepping up MFA, disabling sensitive features, or terminating the session), the adversary proceeds with unconstrained exploitation.

metadata.title: Probing Application-Layer Misuse Thresholds and Active Defenses
attack_steps: Establish an authenticated low-privilege session.
Execute cross-role authorization probes to generate 403 Forbidden events.
Submit malformed JSON/XML payloads and parameters with duplicate keys.
Introduce rapid method switching and sudden User-Agent or IP geo-location transitions.
Monitor application behavior to see if countermeasures (CAPTCHAs, progressive delays, step-up MFA, or session invalidation) are triggered.

text: Pattern: Unexpected File Type Ingestion and Web Execution Root Escalation. 1) Executable Code Placement: In an image-sharing feature expecting .jpg/.gif, an attacker submits a server-side script (.php, .jsp, .asp) or an active document (.html containing JavaScript) with a spoofed image MIME type ('image/jpeg'). The server moves the payload to a publicly accessible directory without renaming or stripping executable permissions, enabling direct code execution or stored XSS. 2) Zip Slip / Path Traversal via Compressed Uploads: In archive or batch upload processing, an attacker uploads a ZIP file containing files with directory traversal path names (e.g., ../../var/www/shell.php), extracting unauthorized files into arbitrary filesystem locations. 3) Semantic Format Corruption: Uploading structurally incompatible file types (e.g., submitting an arbitrary database file where a CSV/XLSX is expected) causing parsing exceptions, unhandled state corruptions, or database misalignment.

metadata.title: File Type Evasion, Script Upload, and Archive Traversal
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
metadata.state_transition: UPLOAD_FORM_ACCESSED -> FORGED_FILE_SUBMITTED (MIME Spoofed) -> SERVER_STORAGE_PERSISTED -> DIRECT_RESOURCE_REQUESTED -> CODE_EXECUTION
attack_steps: Identify file upload endpoints and enumerate business-approved file extensions.
Craft non-approved payloads (e.g., .php, .jsp, .html, .exe) and test upload.
Bypass client-side JavaScript validation via intercepting proxy.
Spoof the 'Content-Type' request header to match an approved MIME type (e.g., image/png).
Inspect whether direct URL access executes or serves the raw script.
Test archive uploads containing directory traversal sequences (Zip Slip) in internal file paths.

text: Pattern: Multi-Vector Malicious File Ingestion and Server Compromise. 1) Polyglot & Web Shell Deployment: An attacker bypasses server extension checks via case alteration (file.PhP), alternative executable extensions (file.phtml, .php5, .shtml, .aspx, .cshtml), trailing delimiters/null bytes (file.php%00.jpg, file.asp...), or Nginx path confusion (test.jpg/x.php), deploying a remote execution shell within web-accessible paths. 2) Zip Slip Archive Traversal: An attacker uploads a valid ZIP archive containing nested traversal paths (..\..\..\shell.php) to overwrite critical system files or drop scripts into the webroot upon backend extraction. 3) Resource Exhaustion via Decompression Bomb: An attacker uploads an archive yielding an extreme decompression ratio (e.g., 1MB expanding to 1GB or multi-level recursion quines), exhausting disk space or memory and disrupting service. 4) Weaponized Document Payloads: Injecting formula macros into CSVs, macro code into Office docs, or embedded JavaScript into PDFs.

metadata.title: Web Shell Execution, Archive Traversal, and Decompression Bombs
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
attack_steps: Map file processing pipelines, parsing libraries, and storage locations.
Test extension filtering boundaries using alternative extensions (.phtml, .shtml), case manipulation, and trailing character injections.
Upload EICAR standard test string or Metasploit test artifacts to evaluate AV/antimalware integration.
Construct ZIP archives containing path traversal tokens (..\..\) to test directory containment during extraction.
Evaluate decompression bomb resilience with high-ratio compressed payloads.
Verify remote code execution by requesting the uploaded payload URL with execution query parameters (e.g., ?cmd=cat+/etc/passwd).

text: Pattern: Common Business Logic and Workflow Abuse Patterns. 1) Price/Quantity Manipulation: Injecting negative item quantities, client-specified price overrides, or switching currency parameters mid-transaction while retaining the absolute numeric amount. 2) State Traversal and Step Skipping: Directly calling post-verification or terminal completion endpoints (e.g., /checkout/complete, /kyc/verify) to advance workflow state without fulfilling prerequisite actions. 3) TOCTOU Race Condition Exploitation: Dispatching synchronized concurrent requests (e.g., via HTTP/2 multiplexing) to execute check-then-act sequences (such as double-spending account balances, replaying single-use vouchers, or exceeding inventory reservations). 4) Circular Value Dispensing Abuse: Multi-accounting or self-referral abuse where automated accounts harvest sign-up bonuses, stack incompatible discount codes, or repeatedly cycle free trial access.

metadata.title: Representative Business Logic Abuse and State Violation Scenarios
metadata.source: OWASP Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet
attack_steps: Identify operations relying on client input for calculations or workflow gating.
Map multi-stage workflows to identify state check endpoints and dependency chains.
Test parameter mutation (e.g., negative values, altered currency tags, hidden field overrides).
Dispatch parallel race requests against single-use or balance-deduction endpoints.
Test terminal endpoint invocation without executing predecessor steps.

text: Pattern: State Sequence Subversion and Step Omission (CWE-841). In a multi-stage session (e.g., S0: Init -> S1: Authorize -> S2: Process -> S3: Finalize), the system exposes distinct endpoints for each stage but tracks state transitions naively or relies on client-side navigation. An attacker directly triggers terminal endpoint S3 or reorders requests (S0 -> S3), skipping validation or settlement steps in S1 and S2. This forces the server-side state machine into an unexpected state where actions are executed without satisfying required prerequisites.

metadata.title: Stateful Sequence Skipping and Workflow Desynchronization
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-841: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow
attack_steps: Map multi-step state progression across target endpoints.
Identify endpoints handling terminal state actions (e.g., confirmation, approval, finalization).
Bypass intermediate authorization or payment endpoints by issuing direct HTTP requests to the terminal endpoint.
Evaluate whether the application executes the action without prerequisite completion tokens.

text: Pattern: Interleaved Multi-Thread State Mutation (TOCTOU Race Condition). In a business transaction flow (e.g., wallet withdrawal, promotional voucher redemption, or limited item reservation), the backend executes two decoupled operations: 1) State evaluation (SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = :id), and 2) State commitment (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amount). An attacker dispatches concurrent parallel HTTP requests synchronized within sub-millisecond windows (e.g., via HTTP/2 single-packet multiplexing). Multiple threads pass the pre-condition check simultaneously against the identical baseline state before any individual thread commits the update, resulting in multi-spend or limit exhaustion.

metadata.title: Concurrent TOCTOU Multi-Spend and State Invalidation
attack_steps: Identify critical sections featuring check-then-act logic without explicit locking (e.g., credit redemption, balance deduction).
Craft duplicate state-modifying requests targeting the identical resource identifier.
Synchronize request arrival using connection warming and HTTP/2 multiplexed single-packet delivery.
Verify that multiple competing requests execute concurrently and commit state against stale check results.

text: Pattern: Repetitive Invocation of Restricted Single-Use Operations (CWE-837). An application exposes functionality intended strictly for one-time execution per actor (e.g., submitting a rating, casting a ballot, claiming a registration voucher, or reserving a seat). The backend relies on client-side state flags (such as browser cookies or localStorage), unverified session parameters, or non-persisted in-memory caches to record participation. An attacker modifies or clears client tokens, cycles session handles, or uses automated HTTP request replay to submit the restricted operation repeatedly. The system increments metrics, allocates duplicate inventory, or dispenses compounding credits without verifying prior historical execution against an authoritative database record.

metadata.title: Single-Use Operation Replay and Uniqueness Bypass
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-837: Improper Enforcement of a Single, Unique Action
attack_steps: Identify operations intended to execute only once per actor or transaction.
Execute baseline submission and verify initial state persistence.
Inspect request/response headers for ephemeral tracking tokens (e.g., cookie-based vote tracking).
Clear cookies, regenerate session headers, or replay raw POST requests via proxy tools.
Submit successive payloads targeting the identical unique entity.
Verify whether downstream counters, balances, or resource locks increment repeatedly.

text: Pattern: Execution Logic Subversion via Behavioral and Order-of-Operations Flaws. An application relies on implicit control-flow assumptions where security gates, parsing routines, and state actions execute in a decoupled or flawed sequence. Common exploitation variants include: 1) Authorization Before Canonicalization (CWE-551): Access control policies evaluate raw URI/parameter paths before downstream URL decoding or path canonicalization, allowing attackers to access protected administrative controllers via encoded directory traversal or dot-segments. 2) Execution After Redirect (EAR, CWE-698): A controller issues an HTTP 302 redirect for unauthenticated sessions but fails to terminate script execution (missing return/exit), permitting unauthorized backend state modifications to proceed. 3) Fall-Through Logic Bypass (CWE-484): Missing break statements in dispatch switches cause execution to cascade into privileged administration handlers.

metadata.title: Behavioral Flow Inversion and Unchecked Execution Anomalies
attack_steps: Map target application request pipelines and identify the ordering of canonicalization, authentication, and execution.
Submit encoded path representations (e.g., /%2e%2e/admin) to test if authorization checks evaluate raw strings while downstream routing decodes them.
Test redirect responses (HTTP 302) to verify whether server processes body-level state modifications after issuing the redirect.
Audit control-flow dispatchers for missing break statements or incorrect boolean operator precedence.

text: Pattern: Unthrottled Interaction Replay and Resource Exhaustion (CWE-799). An application relies on client-side UI disabling, CAPTCHA rendering exclusively in the browser DOM, or superficial IP-based limits that fail to inspect per-token or per-session velocities. An attacker scripts automated request pipelines (e.g., via Turbo Intruder or custom headless workers) to dispatch bursts of business-critical requests (e.g., /cart/apply-coupon, /auth/login, /api/referrals, /vote). Because the backend server lacks sliding-window rate limiters, token-bucket controls, or interaction quotas, each successive request is processed synchronously, leading to stacked business benefits, computational denial of service, or authentication enumeration.

metadata.title: Automated High-Frequency Interaction Replay and Resource Depletion
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-799: Improper Control of Interaction Frequency
attack_steps: Identify sensitive business operations susceptible to automation or brute force.
Probe endpoint velocity thresholds by transmitting incremental request bursts without user pacing.
Evaluate whether client-side rate limits or CAPTCHAs can be bypassed by directly addressing the back-end API route.
Scale request concurrency to measure resource exhaustion or observe state corruption (e.g., coupon stacked repeatedly).

text: Pattern: Execution Logic Subversion via Inadequate Control Flow Management. 1) Unchecked Synchronization / Mutex Failures: A critical section attempts resource locking (e.g., pthread_mutex_lock) but ignores error return codes, continuing execution into shared data manipulation and causing race conditions or undefined state. 2) Scoping and Block Delimitation Omissions: Missing block delimiters (e.g., Apple 'goto fail' style scoping defects or omitted curly braces in condition branches) cause sensitive execution steps or state transitions to execute unconditionally regardless of prior validation checks. 3) Premature Resource Ingestion / Early Processing: Ingestion logic loads heavy resources into memory or triggers external processing before evaluating whether the requesting identity is authorized to access the resource.

metadata.title: Execution Logic Alteration and Scoping Mismanagement Patterns
associated_capec: CAPEC-29: Leveraging Time-of-Check and Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) Race Conditions
attack_steps: Identify operations where execution order, scoping, or synchronization determines security logic.
Inject unexpected inputs or concurrency bursts that cause synchronization mechanisms to fail or return non-zero error states.
Observe whether downstream critical sections execute despite upstream synchronization or condition failures.
Exploit premature processing by issuing high volumes of unauthorized resource requests to induce denial of service.

text: Pattern: Security Bypass and Resource Exhaustion via Order-of-Operation Inversion (CWE-696). 1) Validation Before Canonicalization (CWE-179): An application verifies whether a supplied file path begins with a permitted prefix (e.g., path.startsWith('/safe_dir/')) prior to resolving dot-segments. An attacker supplies '/safe_dir/../etc/passwd', passing prefix validation before canonicalization resolves the path to the root directory. 2) Resource Allocation Before Authorization (CWE-1280): An endpoint reads a large target file or executes an intensive database extraction prior to checking user authorization. While the response body is withheld upon authorization failure, the server incurs severe I/O and memory overhead. 3) Privilege Revocation Inversion: An execution handler attempts privilege reduction but executes setuid() prior to setgid(), preventing gid revocation and leaving child processes running with unintended system privileges.

metadata.title: Canonicalization Inversion, Post-Access Authorization, and Privilege Drop Sequencing
attack_steps: Map execution pipelines across ingestion, canonicalization, authorization, and sink operations.
Submit inputs containing traversal sequences, double-encoding, or special characters to verify whether allowlist checks evaluate raw strings.
Probe endpoints with large unauthorized requests to measure memory/CPU consumption before 401/403 responses are issued.
Inspect binary or script routines for privilege drop sequencing (setgid preceding setuid).

text: Pattern: Execution Logic Bypass via Control Flow Scoping and Redirection Fall-Through (CWE-705). 1) Execution After Redirect (EAR): An access control filter checks client authorization; failing the check, it issues an HTTP 302 redirect header to a login/error URL but omits an immediate exit or return call. The interpreter continues executing the remainder of the script, generating server status reports, querying confidential backend databases, or committing unauthorized modifications before the request terminates. 2) Unhandled Exception Scoping / Denial of Service: Critical operations catch generic exceptions or invoke hard termination methods (e.g., System.exit()) within shared server container threads, crashing the application worker or triggering recursive crash/boot loops. 3) Scoping and Block Delimitation Omission: The famous Apple 'goto fail' bug (CVE-2014-1266) where an extra goto statement outside properly scoped blocks caused subsequent signature verification routines to be entirely skipped, failing open and returning success.

metadata.title: Execution After Redirect and Scoping Bypass Patterns
attack_steps: Identify authorization check routines that issue client-side or HTTP redirects upon failure.
Submit unauthenticated or unauthorized requests using an intercepting proxy (preventing automated client-side redirect following).
Inspect the raw HTTP response body to observe if sensitive data or status telemetry is appended after the HTTP 302/301 headers.
Submit parameters triggering edge-case state updates to assess if persistent backend mutations occur despite receiving a redirection status code.
Audit exception blocks for premature process termination or unhandled bubble-ups that crash shared container contexts.

text: Pattern: Unrestricted Credential Guessing and Concurrency Bypass (CWE-307). 1) Dictionary and Password Spraying: An attacker leverages automated password-guessing tools to transmit thousands of common credentials against single target accounts or rotates through user lists with single passwords. Because the server lacks failed-attempt thresholds or account lockout, the account is eventually compromised. 2) Parallel Connection Tarpit Bypass: The application attempts rate limiting by adding artificial delays (e.g., sleep(2000)) to failed authentication handler functions. An attacker circumvents this serialized delay by initiating hundreds of parallel HTTP/TCP connections, multiplying throughput and achieving high aggregate guessing velocity despite per-thread latency.

metadata.title: Credential Guessing, Multi-Connection Flooding, and Delay Bypass
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
attack_steps: Locate authentication endpoints and analyze response behaviors on failed submissions.
Evaluate whether server enforces account lockouts, IP blocks, or CAPTCHA challenges after repeated failures.
If response latency is artificially inflated via sleep/delay, spawn concurrent worker pools to test throughput scalability.
Execute dictionary brute-force or low-and-slow password spraying to identify valid user credentials.

text: Pattern: Exploitation of Foundational Architectural and Logic Omissions (CWE-1348). 1) External Parameter State Manipulation (CWE-472 / CWE-602): An application design accepts sensitive business variables (e.g., unit prices, subscription tiers, role flags, discount totals) via client-controlled request parameters or hidden fields without backend re-derivation, allowing attackers to override transactions. 2) Workflow Step Omission (CWE-841): A multi-stage approval or KYC process lacks an explicit server-side state machine, enabling attackers to directly invoke terminal settlement or provisioning endpoints without completing intermediate checks. 3) Trust Boundary Violation (CWE-501): Unvalidated user-supplied data is written directly into HTTP session attributes or inter-service RPC payloads, altering trust calculations across microservice boundaries. 4) Unbounded Resource Consumption (CWE-799): Value-dispensing operations (promo claims, SMS triggers, gift redemptions) lack architectural rate-limiting and quota controls, exposing the service to automated financial depletion.

metadata.title: Architectural Trust Inversion, Client-State Overrides, and Workflow Gaps
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-1348: OWASP Top Ten 2021 Category A04:2021 - Insecure Design
attack_steps: Examine system architecture to identify where client state is treated as authoritative.
Identify critical check-then-act boundaries and evaluate whether execution gates enforce sequential state progression.
Tamper with supposedly immutable parameters (prices, discounts, approval status, user IDs) in transit.
Bypass client-side gating mechanisms via direct API or microservice endpoint requests.
Evaluate whether repetitive transactions are bounded by database-level quotas and anti-automation controls.
